sentences.text: Australia's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as its trusted supplier of critical minerals: it holds the largest allied position in battery and EV minerals, and 52 economies have it as their best-placed trusted partner for battery minerals.
That is an allied role first: nationally, those two mining steps read Watch and a low-confidence Preserve.
Its domestic industrial effort should go one step down from the mine, into battery materials refining and the rare-earth chain, where it has operating capacity and committed investment to build on.
For battery cells, EV drivetrains, wind turbines and solar inverters it should depend deliberately on trusted producers, which hold more capacity than Australia though not yet enough.
Its development cooperation can help developing partners with credible pathways add that capacity.
The larger domestic task is deployment: storage, grid, wind and solar all need to be built faster, and buying equipment competitively serves that build-out better than localizing it.
The fence that matters is narrow but high: the rare-earth chain, and the control software that can command Australia's grid, batteries, inverters and turbines.

The rare-earth chain from separation to magnets, where China holds 94% of world refining supply and trusted suppliers only 4%; the control software of grid equipment, inverters, batteries and turbines; and the control systems of gas and oil networks.
The answer is qualified trusted supply and control of command paths, not self-sufficiency.
Catch Up in battery materials refining (lithium chemicals, cathode and anode), the best-anchored case for building.
Build rare-earth separation and metal-making on the mining base.
Keep mineral supply reliable for the allies that depend on it: an allied commitment, not a domestic fence.
Battery cells, packs, components and recycling, EV drivetrains and vehicles, wind turbines and their parts, solar inverters, and solar-grade polysilicon.
Source them from trusted producers, such as South Korea, Japan and Poland for battery components and Germany, the United States and Japan for wind parts.
Where allied supply falls short, add trusted capacity through co-investment and, with developing partners, development finance and offtake.
Accelerate battery storage, grid networks, wind and solar power.
Buy commodity hardware competitively from trusted suppliers, with security conditions on equipment that carries built-in control.
Leave open reactors, nuclear fuel and reactor parts, wafers and PV cells, and gas and oil plant equipment.
The color sits in the first two columns, where Australia mines and refines, and in deployment, where it must build faster.
The manufacturing columns are mostly Partner or Watch.

The orange corner flags mark High-fence parts inside other steps: control software in battery, solar, wind, vehicle, grid, gas and oil equipment, and the rare-earth magnets and separation in EV drivetrains and wind.
They are why imported hardware can still sit partly behind a high fence.
Each cell is one supply-chain step of a technology, colored by its strategic choice.
A corner flag marks a mixed step whose named parts sit behind a different fence: in battery cells and packs, the battery software is Secure, the cells Partner and the enclosures Watch.
A dotted outline marks a review case, a call resting on low confidence, a review flag, a thin anchor or a known data artifact; this brief does not turn those calls into recommendations.
lack the data for a call.
Secure is a narrow call for Australia: one whole step and 13 layers inside other steps, which group into the four capabilities below.
Secure does not mean making everything at home.
It means being able to survive a prolonged cutoff or a hostile command, through qualified trusted supply, stocks, redundancy or control of the command path.
Each capability pairs a measured chokepoint or remote command path with assets that Australia or its allies depend on.
The rare-earth chain: separation, metals and magnets
Feeds the magnets of EV motors and wind generators; Australia mines the ore and has operating refining capacity.
China holds 94% of world refining supply and trusted suppliers 4%; substitution is hard and rebuilding takes more than three years.

Scale domestic separation and metal-making on existing capacity and committed investment; build the step to magnets with allied partners through co-investment and offtake; hold stocks until trusted supply qualifies.
Control software of grids, inverters and batteries
Firmware, energy-management and grid-control software can command, update or disable equipment from abroad.
About half the hardware comes from China: 56% of PV module and inverter imports and 49% of battery cells and packs.
Domestic trusted-source and certification rules for firmware, communications and remote access; trusted vendors where control is built into the hardware, as in inverters and battery management.
Remote access to wind turbines and vehicles
Turbine controllers, park control and connected-vehicle software reach large energy assets and fleets from outside the country.
China supplies 53% of wind turbine imports and 36% of EV and charger imports.

Restrictions on remote access and over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors; turbines from trusted makers such as Germany, South Korea and Italy, vehicles from makers such as Germany, the United States and South Korea.
Control systems of LNG terminals and oil and gas pipelines
Australia supplies 12% of world gas and is the best-placed trusted partner of 5 economies for it; terminal and pipeline control can be disrupted remotely.
Control-system risk on assets that Australia and its gas customers depend on.
Domestic rules on access and updates; certified trusted vendors for control systems.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
This is where Australia makes its real industrial choices.
Two questions decide each step: is the capability worth having (Strategic Industrial Value), and how strong is Australia today (Competitive Position)?
No Preserve call clears the evidence bar.
EV mineral mining reads Preserve on a top-quarter Competitive Position, but the call is flagged for review by the engine, and battery mineral mining reads Watch.
The table below treats them as a single capability: the national call stays open, while allies rely on Australia as their largest holder.
What keeps it strategic is reliability and the processing that follows it, not a domestic fence.
Battery materials refining is the clearest case for building.
Its value is high and its position below the top quarter, and it rests on five capability anchors, from operating capacity to committed investment.
China holds 94% of world supply and provides 50% of Australia's imports, so trusted capacity here is scarce for every ally.
Lithium hydroxide and carbonate, cathode and anode materials are all Catch Up.

Rare-earth and wind materials refining and uranium conversion and enrichment also read Catch Up, but they rest on a thin capability anchor (corroborated by context signals only) and a known data artifact; both are review cases, listed in the appendix.
The equipment Australia installs is worth having, but Australia holds almost none of world supply in it and has no capability anchor to build from, so duplicating it would be slow and costly.

Dependence should be deliberate and spread across several trusted producers: Poland, Hungary and the United States for cells and packs, Germany, Japan and Hungary for EV drivetrains, and Germany, the United States and Japan for wind components.
In battery cells and packs, EV drivetrain components, wind turbines, and PV modules and inverters, allied supply falls short, so a purchase-only strategy will not hold.
Solar-grade polysilicon belongs here too: source it deliberately from trusted producers rather than build it.
Some physical capabilities sit in several technology chains, and their calls differ because supply-chain need or evidence differs by technology.
The table keeps the national reading apart from what allies rely on Australia for.

A credible strategy also says what not to localize.
Watch is not a failure: it means affordable, diversified access matters more than domestic production.

Solar is an Accelerate technology, so Australia needs the modules, but making wafers, cells and silicon metal at home adds little strategic value (solar-grade polysilicon, above, is a Partner case); recorded industrial-policy measures run ahead of that case.

The grid must grow faster, but copper and aluminium processing and grid components are Watch steps with low supply-chain need, best bought competitively.

These carry a high value, but nuclear power is not an Australian deployment priority and the supply-chain need is low; keep access open through diversified imports and procurement, not an industry.
In the Allied Industrial Base analysis Australia is a Resource & Processing Anchor, first among allies on share of world resource & processing supply.
It holds 53% of world exports or production of lithium minerals and 25% of rare-earth metals.

It holds a role in five of the ten strategic compacts and a core seat in Nuclear Fuel & Reactor Systems.

New capacity at the best-placed allied hosts, led by Germany, would restore about US$4.7 billion of it a year.

Each technology is split into six supply-chain stages, and each step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order:
Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured;
at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches 60;
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (75) and either Strategic Industrial Value (bar 60) or supply-chain need (bar 67) is high;
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;
Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed.
A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar.
Observed policy never decides a choice.

The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.
